questions.q: If 4 pens cost 20 rupees, what is the ratio of pens to cost?
questions.a: The ratio is 4:20, which simplifies to 1:5. A wrong answer (like 5:1) shows the student confused the order of quantities, putting cost before quantity.

questions.q: If you travel 10 km in 2 hours, how far will you travel in 4 hours? Explain why.
questions.a: You will travel 20 km. This is because the time doubled, so the distance must also double to maintain the same speed (ratio). A wrong answer suggests the student doesn't see the multiplicative relationship between the two quantities.

questions.q: If 3 kg of apples cost 150 rupees, how much will 7 kg of apples cost?
questions.a: Step 1: Find cost of 1 kg (150/3 = 50 rupees). Step 2: Multiply by 7 kg (50 * 7 = 350 rupees). A wrong answer usually comes from adding numbers instead of multiplying/dividing by the ratio.

questions.q: Two quantities A and B are in direct proportion. If A doubles, what happens to B?
questions.a: B must also double. An incorrect answer shows the student does not understand that "direct" means they change by the same factor.

questions.q: If 5 workers can finish a job in 10 hours, is this direct proportion? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, because as the number of workers increases, the time taken decreases (inverse proportion). A student who says "yes" assumes all related quantities are in direct proportion.

questions.q: Create a real-world scenario where two things are in direct proportion and explain your reasoning.
questions.a: Example: "The number of pages I read vs. the time taken." Reasoning: The more time I spend reading, the more pages I finish, and the rate (pages/minute) stays roughly constant. A poor answer would describe something where one does not affect the other or they change inversely.
